===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN =====
**Codex (QA & Risk · Skeptic) — Round 1**

App Store positioning: “Recall is a deterministic, offline-first iOS flashcard trainer for people who want reliable spaced-repetition over hype, with local SM-2 scheduling and clear statements of what the app does and does not do.” The core promise should stay: exact due-card logic by local day, no cloud-synced progress, no fabricated progress states, and a single clean path for “review what is due now.”

The cleanest launch story for App Store is “fast, honest study loop + visible limitations”: on a fresh install, users can create decks and cards, run a full reveal/grade review cycle, and see truthful stats and empty states. That is stronger than trying to describe future-features we do not have wired yet. The biggest risk is to claim anything in marketing that the build does not currently execute (especially reminders scheduling and CSV/Paywall paths). That risk must be explicitly prevented in copy, screenshots, and release notes.

Screenshot/storyboard plan should be a storyboard of the real shipped flow plus explicit gap/limitation visibility, not placeholder imagery. Capture at least these real screens (and all reachable substates): initial launch loading and recovery safety screen, Study empty state “No decks yet,” Deck list with at least one deck and due badge, Card editor with fast keyboard entry, active review card reveal/grade staircase with a visible safe exit, completed-session summary screen, Stats empty state, Stats sparse state after one session, Stats loaded with forecast/history/retention, Settings home with explicit CSV/Demo placeholders, Reminders permission/time UI, Gap & Limitations screen, and the app state when review permission is denied. For App Store storyboard, pair one clean no-data set and one populated set so the honesty claim is obvious in visual evidence.

Privacy label notes are already represented by an on-disk `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`: UserDefaults and FileTimestamp APIs are declared with reasons, and tracking is explicitly false with no collected data types listed. There is no analytics, ads, social features, or third-party network telemetry in the shipped code. The app still uses optional local notifications; there is no external tracking and no sensitive API family currently in use, so no additional privacy categories should be added beyond what is actually accessed.

Permission copy status: Reminder permission is optional and localized to the Settings Reminders screen, with current UI stating “No backend data is used. Reminders are purely local,” and denial guidance that points to system settings. The strongest App Store-facing copy should preserve this exact honesty and avoid implying automatic scheduling. Current reminders preference writes persist (`AppStorage`) but no scheduler service exists yet, so the permission/request flow should be presented as “preference-only” until scheduling is implemented. Add one explicit supportable sentence in the screen and marketing copy: “You can set a time and permission here; scheduled notification delivery is currently implemented only when the reminder scheduler lane is finished.”

Subscription/paywall review risks are high because Free/Plus was part of the locked spec but there is no Plan/Subscription/StoreKit implementation in the app and no `.storekit` config file in the repo. If paywall is reintroduced for launch, App Review risk rises unless the implementation is explicit and compliant: real paywall behavior, StoreKit entitlement verification, Restore Purchases, privacy policy + terms links, and bounded offline error handling. At present, shipping a fake or disabled upgrade affordance would be a rejection and trust-risk issue; the safest launch path is to omit paywall UI entirely or mark it clearly as intentionally unavailable.

Permission and compliance specifics: no additional Info.plist usage strings are currently visible for storage/network/contacts/camera/etc., and none are needed by shipped code paths, but do verify final Info.plist contents during final build verification so no accidental API usage appears without usage text. Notification permissions are user-initiated and should remain that way. If CSV import/export UI is enabled later, file-picker access paths must include clear failure-safe behavior and no hidden network assumptions.

Support/contact requirement is a real launch blocker: there is no in-app support/contact path or legal-links screen today, so App Store metadata and Help/support channel are incomplete. Add an explicit support screen in Settings (email or support URL) and a short FAQ row for offline-only scope and known limitations. Also align on a privacy policy stub + terms page if any policy/ToS references appear in submission.

Age/content risk is low; this is educational/study tooling with no mature themes, no user-generated media, and no social or web content. The primary non-age risk is reliability/trust, not content.

Launch blockers are clear and should block a “store-ready” declaration until addressed: placeholder-only CSV Export and Demo Data are not yet real user features, reminder scheduling service is still absent, StoreKit/Plan path is absent, and the XCUITest + unit verification is not fully green in this environment (`ReviewSessionViewModelTests.swift` has the known main-actor-isolated initializer mismatch at compile time in verification notes, and test execution is not currently reliable from this environment). The app is coherent as an internal milestone, but App Store readiness is blocked by those gaps and by missing support/legal entry points.

**Claude (Delivery Lead · Pragmatist) — Round 1**

Here's my read, coming at this purely from "what can we actually defensibly submit right now."

The single biggest call this phase needs to make isn't about screenshots or copy — it's whether we submit with a Plus/subscription tier or not, and I think the answer is obviously no. There is no StoreKit code, no Plan/Subscription screen, no product IDs, nothing — six-plus build waves and it never got built. Every earlier phase locked Free/Plus as a must-have, but "must-have per the design doc" and "must-have to submit this build" are different questions, and the pragmatic move is to decouple them. If App Store Connect metadata or the app description mentions a paid tier that doesn't exist in the binary, that's a guaranteed metadata-mismatch rejection, and even if it did exist, a rushed StoreKit integration is exactly the kind of thing that trips 3.1.2 (missing terms/privacy links, no functioning Restore Purchases, broken offline-purchase handling) — this project's own architecture phase already flagged all of that as real work, none of which happened. So my recommendation is: ship v1 as a fully free app, zero mention of Plus/subscription/pricing tiers anywhere in App Store copy or in-app UI, and push monetization to a v1.1 submission once StoreKit is actually built and tested. This isn't a scope retreat, it's just refusing to market something that isn't in the binary — the PlanGate stub is already hardcoded unlimited, so functionally nothing breaks by doing this.

Second call: the Reminders screen is a real, if small, problem — not just a "gap." A gap is CSV import routing to an honest "not yet available" screen; that's fine, it says what it is. Reminders is different: the toggle, permission prompt, and time picker all work and *look* like a completed feature, and a user who sets a 9am reminder will reasonably believe a notification is coming. It never will, because there's no `ReminderScheduler` anywhere in the codebase. That's not an honest empty state, that's a UI promising a real notification that silently never fires — which is exactly the class of thing this project's own hard rule against fabricated success states was written to prevent. Given it only needs `UNUserNotificationCenter` (already an approved framework, no new dependency, no infra problem), I'd treat "build the minimal scheduler" as a pre-launch must, not a nice-to-have — it's small, bounded, native-only work, unlike CSV/Demo-Data/StoreKit which are bigger lifts. If for some reason that can't land before submission, the fallback is to pull the Reminders row from Settings entirely for v1 rather than ship it half-true.

Third, practically: `RecallTests/ReviewSessionViewModelTests.swift` still fails to compile on a main-actor-isolation error in a `(plan:service:...)` initializer. This does not block Apple's review — test targets aren't submitted — but it blocks *our* ability to claim the interruption-safety guarantee is proven rather than hand-traced, and given that's the single claim this whole app is built around, I don't think we should let "App Store ready" get declared while our own automated proof of it doesn't even compile. It reads like a small, mechanical fix (likely a missing `@MainActor` or an `await`/`Task` wrapper at a call site), and it should get fixed before we call this phase closed, independent of App Store mechanics.

On the actual required outputs:

**Positioning:** "Recall — the flashcard app that never lies to you." Lead with offline-forever, zero accounts, zero ads, a provably-correct SM-2 engine, not feature breadth. Subtitle candidate: "Spaced repetition, fully offline." Target the exact niche this project has been building for — people who've used Anki/Quizlet and are tired of sync friction, accounts, and engagement-bait. Do not lead with Stats/charts or any Plus-tier language.

**Screenshots:** the honest constraint here is that Demo Data was never built, so a truly fresh install has empty everything. For App Store assets specifically (not the shipped app), we need someone to manually seed a couple of decks with a few weeks of real review history through the actual UI, purely to capture screenshots — Study tab with due counts, mid-review-session with the grade staircase visible, a completed Session Summary, the Stats overview with a populated 30-day forecast chart, and — I'd actually include the Gap & Limitations screen as one of the shots, since "we tell you exactly what this app doesn't do" is a legitimate differentiator for this audience, not something to hide. Dark mode gets at least one paired shot given how central that palette is to the design language.

**Privacy label:** this should be close to the simplest possible label — no accounts, no network, no third-party SDKs, no analytics. Data Not Collected across every category. The only thing to double check against the real build (not just the architecture doc's intent) is that `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` actually exists and lists the Required Reason API usage — `UserDefaults` for the reminder-time preference, and whatever SwiftData/file-timestamp API category applies to the local store. That needs direct confirmation from the build, not another restated decision.

**Permission copy:** the only system permission in this app is notifications, and it's already correctly gated behind the user turning Reminders on rather than firing at cold launch — good, keep that. No Info.plist usage-description string is required for notifications specifically (that's only for camera/location/contacts/etc., none of which this app touches), so there's nothing to write copy for beyond the in-app explanation of why we're asking, which should say plainly "so we can tell you how many cards are due" — no card content, no deck names, matching the already-locked notification-content rule.

**Subscription/paywall review risk:** as above — the resolution is not to have one in this submission. That collapses this entire risk category to zero for v1.

**Launch blockers, concretely, in priority order:** (1) decide and lock "v1 ships free, no Plus copy anywhere" as an actual release decision, not just an assumption; (2) build the minimal local ReminderScheduler or pull the Reminders UI — don't ship a promise that silently fails; (3) fix the ReviewSessionViewModelTests compile error so the interruption-safety claim has a real green test, not just hand-tracing; (4) confirm PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy is actually present in the built artifact; (5) stand up a real support contact — right now I don't see one anywhere (no support URL, no in-app contact), and App Store Connect requires a working support URL at submission; (6) get real screenshots from manually-seeded data since there's no Demo Data feature to lean on. CSV import/export wiring is a should-fix, not a blocker — the parser is solid and tested, it's genuinely just Settings plumbing, but if time is short it can ship as the honest placeholder it already is without creating any review risk, since it doesn't misrepresent anything.

Age rating is straightforward: 4+, no user-generated content, no web content, no third-party account linking, nothing that trips any content category.

My biggest worry about my own recommendation: pulling Plus/subscription from this submission means the monetization work from per_app_product_brief effectively gets shelved indefinitely unless someone explicitly schedules a v1.1 build pass for it — "ship free for now" has a way of becoming permanent. I'd rather say that plainly now than let it happen by default.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Here's where things stand after round one: Codex and I actually agree on more than it might look like at first glance. We both landed on the same core positioning ("never lies to you," offline-forever, provably-correct SM-2, no engagement bait), the same privacy story (Data Not Collected, PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy already exists and is accurate, zero third-party/analytics), the same permission-copy stance (notifications only, user-initiated, count-only body text — don't change anything there), and — most importantly — we both independently concluded the app should **not** ship with any subscription/Plus/paywall marketing or UI in this submission, since there's no StoreKit code, no `.storekit` file, and no Plan screen anywhere in six-plus build waves. That's a real, load-bearing agreement: v1 goes out free, full stop, no "coming soon" Plus language anywhere.

Where we genuinely split, and need another round to resolve:

1. **Whether the honest CSV-export/Demo-Data placeholders count as launch blockers.** Codex's blocker list lumps them in alongside reminders and StoreKit as reasons this isn't "store-ready" yet. I don't think that's right — a placeholder that clearly says "not yet available" doesn't misrepresent anything to Apple or to users, so it shouldn't gate the readiness verdict the way a broken promise would. This needs to be settled explicitly rather than left ambiguous.

2. **What to do about Reminders.** This is the sharper disagreement. Codex treats it as a documented limitation — add one clarifying sentence, ship as-is. I think it's a materially different case than CSV/Demo-Data: the toggle, permission prompt, and time picker all *work* and look complete, so a user who sets a 9am reminder reasonably expects a notification, and none will ever arrive because no `ReminderScheduler` exists. That's closer to a false promise than an honest gap. My position is either build the minimal scheduler before submission (it's small, native-only, `UNUserNotificationCenter`, no new dependency) or pull the Reminders row from Settings entirely for v1 — not ship it half-true. We need to pick one of those, not split the difference with softer copy.

Both of us also flagged the same two mechanical items as needing action regardless: get `ReviewSessionViewModelTests.swift` compiling again (so the interruption-safety claim has a real test, not just hand-tracing), and stand up an actual support/contact path, since neither exists today and App Store Connect requires a working support URL at submission.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs to settle: (a) does an honest placeholder ever count as a launch blocker, or only a broken/misleading feature does; (b) Reminders — fix it, cut it, or ship it with disclosure — pick one; and factor in the project's own fixed tiebreaker (SM-2 correctness > review-flow speed > honest empty states) since this is fundamentally an honesty-vs-shippability call.

===== YOUR TURN — this is Claude talking (round 2) =====

===== YOUR HAT THIS PHASE =====
Come at this as a Delivery Lead — your lens is sequencing, dependencies, who owns what, and a realistic path to done. And bring the temperament of the Pragmatist: fixate on the smallest thing that actually ships and on the real constraints (time, effort, platform limits). This is your stance for THIS phase only — lean into it and don't be a yes-man.
Continue the discussion: react to the new messages by name, defend or update your position, and push toward the best answer for this phase.
Prepare the app for App Store review: positioning, screenshots, privacy labels, permission strings, subscription/paywall review risks, support contact, age/content risks, release blockers, and concrete launch copy.

How to talk in this room:
- Write in plain, natural English, like you're in a lively group chat with two
  sharp friends. NO headings, NO numbered rubrics, NO 0-100 scores, NO
  bullet-point templates, NO sign-off line. Just talk like a person.
- Speak as exactly ONE person (yourself). Don't write the others' messages.
- Go deep and be specific. Make a real argument with concrete examples and think
  out loud. A couple of rich paragraphs, not a shallow blurb.
- React to what the others actually just said, by name (Codex / Claude /
  Gemini / any local model in the room / and the human if they chimed in).
  Quote or paraphrase their point, then build on it or push back on it.
- Genuinely try to CONVINCE the group of whatever you think is the single best
  idea right now — it does NOT have to be your own. If someone makes a better
  case, say so and change your mind out loud.
- Do NOT agree just to agree. If an idea is weak, explain why. Surface the real
  trade-offs and disagreements — that friction is the whole point.
- Make the decisions yourselves; don't punt to "the human."
response:
Codex, I want to zero in on the reminders disagreement because I think it's the one thing actually worth another round of debate, and I want to push back specifically on the "one clarifying sentence" fix. You're framing it as a documented-limitation problem, same bucket as CSV/Demo-Data, just needs better copy. I don't think that's the right bucket, and here's the sharper version of why: a documented limitation is something like the Gap & Limitations screen saying "iCloud backup restore across two devices can produce diverging stores" — it's disclosure about an edge case a user wouldn't discover by normal use. Reminders isn't that. A user actively flips a toggle, grants a system permission, picks 9am, and the UI accepts all of it as if the action completed. The failure isn't in an edge case three screens away, it's baked into the primary interaction itself. Burying "scheduled delivery isn't implemented yet" in body copy on that same screen doesn't fix that — it just means the user has to read fine print to un-believe what the interactive controls just told them. That's a worse trust pattern than an honest empty state, not a better one, and it's a strange thing to ship in an app whose entire personality is "we don't do that to you."

Here's where I actually want to resolve this cleanly rather than let it be a vibes argument: we have a standing, already-locked tiebreaker for exactly this kind of dispute — SM-2 correctness, then review-flow speed, then honest empty states, in that order, no exceptions. Run CSV export/Demo-Data through that lens and they pass cleanly: both are implemented today as honest placeholders that say plainly "not yet available." That's not a violation of priority #3, that's priority #3 working exactly as designed. So I'm dropping my earlier hedge — Codex, you're right that they're real, tracked incompleteness against the original six-feature spec, and I'm not pretending otherwise, but they are not App Store blockers and they should not gate a "store-ready" verdict. They belong in the Gap & Limitations register and in our own internal punch list, not in the launch-blocker section. Now run Reminders through the same lens: it's not an honest empty state, it's a working-looking control that silently produces nothing. That's the one place in this whole app where the tiebreaker's third priority is actually at risk of being violated, which is exactly why it deserves different treatment than CSV or Demo Data, not the same treatment.

So given that, what do we actually do about it — and here's where I want to update my own round-1 position, not just repeat it. I offered two options last round: build the minimal scheduler, or pull the row. I want to drop "build it" as the live option and just commit to pulling it, and the reason is really simple and very on-brand for me as the pragmatist: look at this project's actual track record on this exact feature. Nine-plus separate iterations across build_coordination and write_tests waves had a participant confidently narrate a fully-working ReminderScheduler that turned out, every single time, to not exist on disk. That's not bad luck, that's a pattern telling us this specific piece of work is harder to actually land than it looks on paper, or at least harder than this room's history suggests anyone's given it credit for. Betting our submission timeline on "this time we'll really build it" is exactly the kind of optimistic scheduling risk a Delivery Lead should refuse to take when there's a nearly-free alternative sitting right there. Pulling the interactive toggle costs us almost nothing — hide the row, replace it with a flat "Reminders: coming in a future update" line or fold it into the Gap register, done in an afternoon, zero new engineering risk, and it's airtight honest. We lose one optional, satellite feature (and the prompt itself calls it "one optional local notification," not core loop) for one release. That's a much better trade than either shipping a quiet lie or gambling more build time on a feature this project has failed to deliver nine times running.

Where I'm fully aligned with you and don't think there's daylight left: the free-only v1 with zero Plus/subscription anywhere, the ReviewSessionViewModelTests compile fix as a must-do before we call this phase's own work done, and the support/contact URL as a genuine submission blocker. I'd also add one thing neither of us said explicitly yet — once we pull Reminders from the shipped Settings screen, we should double check the screenshot plan doesn't include a Reminders shot at all, since there's nothing left there worth showing, and update the App Store description to not mention reminders as a feature. Small thing, but it's exactly the kind of drift that happens when a decision here doesn't get carried through to the actual asset list.

So my actual ask for round 3 or wherever we land consensus: adopt the two-tier blocker framework (App-Store-blocking vs. tracked-gap) with CSV/Demo-Data explicitly in the non-blocking tier, and settle Reminders as "pull the interactive UI for v1, disclose in the Gap register, revisit in v1.1 alongside StoreKit" rather than shipping it with a caveat sentence.
